ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Debt Swap Scheme for States 
*201.   DR.T.SUBBARAMI REDDY:† 
SHRI MOOLCHAND MEENA: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether States have pre-paid Rs. 23,000 crore of high cost debts in the 
first seven months ending October 31,2003 in the current financial year taking 
advantage of the debt-swap scheme; 
(b) if so, whether this pre-payment will also help States in decreasing funds 
and improving State finances; and 
(c) if so, to what extent States have pre-paid their debts uptill now? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (c) A 
Statement is placed on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) No, Sir. States have pre-paid an amount of Rs. 33,507.50 crores of 
outstanding high cost Government of India loans during the current year upto 
end of October, 2003. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) High cost debt of Government of India, amounting to Rs. 49,818 
crores has been pre-paid by the States uptill now. 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Dr. T. Subbarami Reddy. 

RAJYA SABHA        [16 December, 2003] 
DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I would like to know 
from the hon. Finance Minister this. In our country, in almost all the States, or 
in major States, there are financial crises. I welcome this Debt Relief Scheme, 
which is being planned by the Government. But here, I ' would like to know 
which are the States where the progress is very much hampered due to financial 
crises and how to come out from the problem. Are they suffering because of the 
heavy interest burden or due to too much subsidies being given to various 
schemes? Ultimately, what is the Government's plan to bail out states like 
Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and so many other big 
States in the country wher e there are financial crises? May I know from the 
Finance Minister as to what are the cris es, and how they are going to solve the 
problem? As on today, how this debt relief scheme, by reducing the burden of 
interest, is going to bail out the states to some extent? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Sir, the hon. Member has asked rather an 
omnibus question. The very purpose of the Debt Swap Scheme for States is to 
ameliorate the difficulties of the Stat es on account of th e heavy burden of 
debt. We had set out ourselves the target in the Ministry of Finance when I 
started the scheme of doing debt swap of Rs. 114,000 crores in a three-year 
period. I am very glad to share with the House that, in fact in a one-year period 
, spread over two financial years of that 100 odd thousand crores of rupees, we 
have reached almost the Rs. 50,000 crores mark of swapping high-cost debt. In 
the balance two-three months, I expect to reach another Rs. 10-12,000 crores. 
So we will have a total of Rs. 62,000 crores of debt swap against Rs. 114 
thousand which was to be done in three years. The hon. Member wanted to know 
what are the difficulties that some states are experiencing in this regard. Now, 
of course, all the States are participating. In the beginning, Maharashtra did 
not wish to participate because of various reasons. I do not wish to analyse the 
finances of each and every State here in the House. It is also not the purpose 
of the question. But the difficulties that some States have expressed are in 
regard to a possible liquidity shortage  that they may f ace on account of the 
Debt Swap Scheme being linked so closely to the small savings. This is broadly 
the answer to the hon. Member's question. 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Mr. Chairman, I am happy, the hon. 
Finance Minister on 14th, that is, day before yesterday, announced that

Management of Kolkata Stock Exchange 
*202. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister 
of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a)   whether Government have noticed deficiencies in the management 
of Kolkata Stock Exchange; 
5 

RAJYA SABHA        [16 December, 2003] 
(b) if so, the steps being taken to streamline the working of the 
Exchange; and 
(c) what steps SEBI is taking to ensure normal working of stock 
Exchanges? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (c) A 
Statement is placed on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) SEBI has superceded the Committee of Calcutta Stock Exchange on 
December 4,2003 for a period of one year and appointed Shri Tushar Kanti Das, 
IAS (retd.) as administrator of the exch ange to exercise and perform all the 
powers and duties of the Committee. 
(c) In order to remove operational, market and systemic risks SEBI has 
taken following major steps to ensure normal working of the stock exchanges. 
(1) Issued orders in January 2002 specifying that no broker member 
of the stock exchanges shall be an  office bearer of an exchange i.e. 
hold the positio of President, Vice President, Treasurer, etc. 
(2) Advised the exchanges to have time bound arbitration proceedings. 
(3) Exchanges have been advised to submit a scheme of corporatisation 
and demutulization. To facilitate the process, a Bill to amend the Securities 
Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 has been introduced in the Parliament on 
August 19, 2003 and is presently being examined by the Standing Committee 
on Finance. 
(4) Advised the stock exchanges that no broker director shall be 
authorized to sign any cheques or operate any bank accounts on behalf of the 
stock exchange. 
(5) Issued model bye-laws, in October, 2003, which would be applicable 
to all exchanges. 
(6) Introduced shorter settlement cycles. 
(7) Started holding weekly surveillance meetings with stock exchanges 
and depositories.

*203. SHRI R.S. GAVAI: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have examined the recommendations made by

RAJYA SABHA        [16 December, 20U3] 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The Working Group constituted by the Government studied 
various aspects of the petroleum and natural gas sector in the context of 
liberalisation of the sector as well as its increasing exposure to international oil 
market. It made a number of recommendations which include strengthening of 
oil security through accelerated exploration programmes, acquisition of equity 
oil abroad, development of alternative so urces of fuels, creation of strategic 
reserves of oil/product and product qua lity improvement for environmental 
protection. Accordingly, the following action plans have been approved by 
the Government under the Tenth Five Year Plan: 
(i) Acceleration of exploration effort s especially in deep offshore and 
frontier areas. 
(ii) Launching of Improved Oil Recovery (IOR) & Enhanced Oil 
Recovery (EOR) programmes. 
(iii)  Enhancing efforts for securing equity oil and gas abroad. 
(iv)  Creation of strategic storage facilities for crude oil. 
(v) Development of alternate fuels including Coal Bed Methane, Motor Spirit-
Ethanol Blend and Gas Hydrates. In addition, the government is also 
implementing Bio-Diesel programmes. 
(vi) Implementation of Product Quality Improvement Projects by Oil PSUs 
for meeting prescribed environmental standards.

RAJYA SABHA        [16 December, 2003] 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI 
RAM NAIK): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Some incidents of supply of under-weight cylinders to 
customers by way of pilferage of gas from Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) 
cylinders have come to the notice of the Government. Following measures are 
being taken to prevent pilferage of LPG from cylinders:- 
(i) Liquefied Petroleum Gas (Regulation of Supply and Distribution) 
Order, 2000 under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 has been 
promulgated. As per this Order, pilfering product from cylinder/ 
supply of partially used cylinder to LPG consumer by the distributors 
of Public Sector Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) as well as Parallel 
Marketeers has been prohibited. Such offence is punishable with 
imprisonment from 3 months to 7 years under the Essential 
Commodities act. 
(ii) State Governments are empowered  to take action against the erring 
distributors under the provisions of the above Order. 
(iii) Marketing Discipline Guidelines (MDG) for LPG distributors of 
OMCs have been laid down by the Government in April, 2001. 
According to these guidelines, in  case of establishment of any 
complaint of pilferage/supply of pa rtially used cylinders to customer, 
a fine of Rs. 20,000 plus the price the LPG pilfered/ supplied short at 
commercial rate for 1 st offence, Rs. 50,000 plus the price of LPG 
pilfered/supplied short at commerc ial rate for 2nd offence, and 
termination for 3rd offence by the distributor is imposed. 
(iv) LPG distributors of OMCs are under strict insturctions to supply the 
cylinders of right quantity to their customers. The officials of OMCs 
carry out random checks at distributor's godown, delivery point as well 
as enroute to ensure that no pilferage takes place. On the establishment 
of any complaint of pilferage or supply of partially used cylinder to 
customer, action against the erring distributor is taken in terms of 
MDG and/or Distributorship Agreement.

OMCs have reported 12 established cases of pilferage/supply of partially 
used cylinders to customers against their distributors during the period April-
September, 2003.

Chloride (PVC) seals as a tamper evident sealing system for LPG cylinders to 
arrest the theft of gas from cylinders with a view to supply correct weight gas 
to the consumers. PVC seals are difficult to duplicate, shrink at high 
temperature and require special technical expertise to manufacture.

(a) to (c) Government is committed to supply clean and unadulterated fuel

(i)  issuance of Naphtha & Solvents Control Orders, 
(ii)  establishment of Anti-Adulteration Cell (AAC),

stringent, 
(v)   introduction of new tamper proof tank-locking system,

premature failure of car engines were received by the Government. Oil 
Marketing Companies (OMCs) have been directed to be extra vigilant to prevent 
any possibility of adulteration of fuels which can adversely effect the 
performance of vehicular engines. Also, State Government have been 
apprised of the same and requested for necessary investigation and strict 
against Retail Outlets indulging in the adulteration.

 *218.  DR. A.R. KIDWAI: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY:

from November, 23-25, 2003;

global competitiveness report 2003-04 released by the World Economic 
Forum;

India Economic Summit held in New Delhi from November, 23-25, 2003 was 
attended by public personalities, senior government officials and business 
leaders from various countries like Australia, Brazil, China, France, Germany, 
Iran, Netherlands, Singapore, Sri Lanka, Thailand, UK, USA and India. The

international/geopolitical issues, foreign direct investment (FDI), corporate

Credit Policy for Urban Cooperative Banks 
1422. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Reserve Bank of India has announced new credit policy for 
Urban Cooperative Banks; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the Federations of the Urban Cooperative Banks have 
represented against the policy; and 
(d) if so, the details there of and further reaction of Government thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) and (b) In order to provide greater 
flexibility to urban co-operative banks, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) 
proposed in the credit policy 2002-03; 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2003] 
* To withdraw the stipulation of Minimum Lending Rate (MLR) for all 
co-operative banks. Co-operative ba nks are free to determine their 
lending rates taking into account their cost of funds, transaction cost, 
etc. with the approval of their managing committee. 
* To ensure that the interest rate s charged by co-operative banks are 
transparent and known to all their customers, Banks are requested to 
publish the minimum and maximum interest rates charged by them, 
and display this information in every branch. 
Further, with a view to moving towards international best practices and to 
ensure greater transparency, in the mid-term monetary and credit policy 2002-
03, the 90 days norm for recognition of loan impairment has also been made 
applicable to urban co-operative banks and regional rural banks with effect 
from March, 31, 2004. It has been decided to extend the 90 days norm for 
recognition of loan impairment to the State Co-operative Banks and District 
Central Cooperative Banks from the year ending March, 31, 2006. Banks are 
advised to move over to charging interest on monthly rests effective April 1, 
2004 to facilitate smooth transition. Ho wever, the gold loans and small loans 
would continue to be governed by the 180 days norms for classification as 
NPA. 
In regard to loans and advances or other financial accommodation by 
UCBs to their directors, RBI stipulated  that UCBs should not grant loans and 
advances (both secured and unsecured) to directors, their relatives and 
firms/concerns/companies in which they are interested. 
(c) and (d) RBI has reported that the Federations of Urban Cooperative 
Banks have represented against certain measures of the above credit policies. 
The actions taken on some of the important issues are as given below: 
(i) The effective date for ban on fresh advances to Directors, relatives, 
firms/concerns in which they are interested was postponed from 29 
April 2003 to 1 October 2003. 
(ii) UCBs are now allowed to place de posits with strong scheduled urban 
co-operative banks.

has been mentioned that they are exacting an economic cost in terms of 
foregone growth. However, following the excellent monsoon, the IMF has 
since revised its forecast for India's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth

2003) also forecasts a GD.P growth of over 7 per cent based on sound 
macroeconomic fundamentals, bountiful monsoon, moderate inflation and 
strong external sector performance.

precipitation of 102 per cent of Long Period Average (LPA). As a result,

FDI in India as compared to China 
1465. DR. AKHILESH DAS: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) Whether it is a fact that China attracts seven times more of Foreign 
Direct Investment (FDI), according to World Investment Report, 2003; 
(b) if so, how the FDI in India is comp ared to that of China during 2001 
and 2002; 
(c) whether Government have studied the reasons for such a low level of 
FDIs in India, as compared to China; and 
(d) What steps are being taken by Government to improve FDI inflow? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRl 
ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) to (d) Foreign Direct Investment 
flows to developing countries which stood at US $ 238 Billion in 2000, fell to 
US$ 205 Billion in 2001 and further to US$ 190 Billion in 2 002. FDI flows 
into India, however, have not gone down in 2002 despite the global trands. 
128 

[16 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
India's Official statistics on FDl inflow for the relevant years did not 
include reinvested earnings (by foreign companies), inter-company debt 
transactions and overseas commercial borrowings by foreign direct investors 
in foreign invested firms, as per standard IMF definitions.This is in contrast to 
China, which has been reporting FDl following the standard IMF 
nomenclature. 
Owing to the fact that India' s Offical RBI Statistics on FDl 
systematically understates infl ows compared to the accepted IMF 
methodology, the International Finance Corporation has estimated that actual 
FDl inflows into India during 2001 could range between US$ 5 Billion to 
US$ 8 Billion. Furthermore, according to Global Development Finance, 2002, 
'round tripping' [that is flows from Hong Kong into China and vice versa 
accounts for nearly 50% of China's FDl. Both these factors do not reflect a 
fair comparison of official FDl figures between India and China. 
The International Finance Corporation has done an exercise to readjust 
FDl inflows in both India and China, for the sake of comparability. According to 
this exercise, China's FDl to Gross Domestic Product ratio is twice that of 
India's. 
Since mid-2003, reinvested earnings and equity capital of unincorporated 
bodies are being included in FDl data on  an annual basis. The liberal policies 
of the Government is expected to lead to enhanced FDl flows in the future.

Fire in ONGC pipeline 
1499. SHRI MURLI DEORA: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether an undersea pipeline of  ONGC carrying crude oil from 
Mumbai High North oil field Uran (Mumbai) developed a leak in August, 2003 
causing oil spill; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
(c) by when the leak was detected and what is the estimated loss; and 
(d) what impact it had on the environment? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS (SHRIMATI SUMITRA MAHAJAN): (a) to (d) 
Leakage of crude oil was observed from 30 inch oil trunk pipeline from 
Mumbai High to Uran at 1740 hrs on 10th August, 2003. The leakage was 
suspected to be from a small rupture in this cement coated trunk pipeline. 
As per the findings of a high level Committee of ONGC, internal 
corrosion of the pipeline has been found to be the principal cause of the 
leakage. 
The quantity of crude oil spilled was approximately 200 Metric Tons 
(MT).The estimated effect on crude oil production due to non-availability of the 
trunk pipeline and subsequent restriction in production rate till the line was 
repaired, is around 0.171 Million Metric Ton (MMT). 
The oil spill was contained immediately within a few hours. The 
application of chemical dispersant broke down oil slick into patches making 
their effect a localized one. There was insignificant damage to the 
environment, prima facie.

Inter-state meeting for river water disputes 
1542. DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO: Wi ll the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of inter-State meetings held of the basin States to sort out 
the use, distribution or control of water of inter-State rivers in the country, 
during the last three years, year-wise and what are the names of the participating 
States; 
(b) what was the outcome of these inter-State meetings; and 
(c) what steps Government have taken for the amicable settlement of inter-
State river water disputes in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a)The Central 
Government is required to hold inter-State meetings to sort out disputes 
between the States on use, distribution or control of water of inter-State rivers 
in the country under the provisions of the Inter-State River Water Disputes 
Act, 1956. An inter-State meeting of the basin States of Maharashtra, Goa 
and Karnataka was convened by the Union Minister (Water Resources) on 
December 20, 2002 for finding a negotiated settlement of the dispute. 
(b) It was decided in the meeting that Government of Goa and Central Water 
Commission officials will make joint efforts to reconcile the discrepancies in 
the date and yield figures. 
(c) The Union Government makes all efforts to resolve the water 
disputes among the States amicably through negotiations and mutual 
discussion, failing which the disputes are referred to a Tribunal for 
adjudication under the provisions of Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 
1956. The said Act has been amende d in the year 2002, whereby the 
adjudication of the water dispute by a Tribunal has been made time bound.

NATIONAL IMPORTANCE 
SHRI SHANKAR ROY CHOWDHURY (West Bengal): Madam 
Deputy Chairman, through your kindness, I briefly want to raise an issue for 
the attention of this House and the Government. 
Today, the 16,h December, is Vijaya Diwas, on which day in 1971, the 
Pakistani forces in erstwhile East Pakistan, now, Bangladesh, signed an 
Instrument of Surrender at Dhaka acknowledging their unconditional 
capitulation to the Indian Armed Forces. Ninety-three thousand Pakistani 
troops laid down their weapons and were transported into Indian custody 
255 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2003] 
where they were accorded the treatment of Prisoners of War in full accordance 
with the Geneva Convention. It was a gr eat and glorious victory and, I believe, 
one of the defining moments in the hist ory of independent India. If we won our 
independence on 15th August, 1947, and became a Republic on 26 th January, 
1950, I do believe, we came of age as a nation after our historic victory in 
Bangladesh which was formalised on this day in 1971. It was a day whose full 
significance and impact on our march to nationhood is perhaps not yet fully 
understood or appreciated by our people. Perhaps that is why we do not mark 
and honour its importance in a formal and befitting manner perhaps on par 
with other festivals of our nationhoo d like the Independence Day and Republic 
Day. I urge upon the Government to take formal acknowledgement of the 
national importance of this occasion an d institute it as a day of national 
importance to be honoured and observed in a befitting manner by our nation 
and by our people.

THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): Madam, I 
beg to move: 
That the Bill to repeal the Sick Industrial Companies (Special 
Provisions) Act, 1985, as passed by Lok Sabha, be taken into 
consideration. 
Madam, the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 
was enacted to tackle the problem of industrial sickness. The Act has not been 
effective in checking the problem either  of industrial sickness or of finding 
timely solutions for restructuring corporate entities. 
In view of the problems observ ed in the BIFR mechanism, the Sick 
Industrial Companies (Special Provisions ) Bill, 2001 for the repeal of SICA, 
1985 and the abolition of BIFR/Appellate Authority for Industrial & Financial 
Reconstruction was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 30m August 2001. 
Simultaneously, another Bill viz. the Companies (Amend) Bill, 2001 
was introduced in this House to provide an alternative mechanism in lieu of 
BIFR/AAIFR with the main objectiv e of facilitating and expediting 
revival/rehabilitation of si ck companies and protection of workers' interests, 
and also, where necessary, winding up of companies. 
The SICA Repeal Bill was referred to the Standing Committee on 
Finance for examination. The Committee's report to the Parliament, submitted 
on 19th December, 2002, reflected a broa d consensus that BIFR set up under 
SICA had, to a large extent, failed to achieve its objective because of its 
inherent deficiencies. The Standing Committee on Finance recommended that 
the SICA might be repealed; and it also approved the SICA Repeal Bill, 2001. 
The Committee had made certain observations about pending cases abating 
on the repeal of SICA, saying that this had not been addressed in this Bill and 
the Committee had recommended that the Government should bring forward 
suitable amendments in the Bill itself to deal with such cases. 
After considering the Standing Committee's report, the amendments 
in the SICA (SP) Repeal Bill, 2001 were proposed at the time of the 
consideration of the Bill in the Lok Sab ha, to provide for (i) registration of 
abated cases by NCLT and removal of the limitations as to.

BIFR/AAIFR to be monitored by NCLT; and ( iii) for waiver of fee in respect of 
abated cases when they register afresh with NCLT. 
I commend, therefore, Madam, that SICA (Special Provisions) Repeal 
Bill as passed by the Lok Sabha on ,th December, 2003 be taken up for 
consideration and passed.

Now, I come to number three. On the similar basis, "No fresh 
reference, with respect to a sick company, shall be made to the BIFR after the 
Repealing Act, 2001, comes into force." Madam, what is the recommendation 
of the Standing Committee on Finance? What is the comment  of the Standing 
Committee on Finance? The Standing Committee on Finance looked into this 
very elaborately and made its recommendations. I wish to read one of the 
recommendations of the Committee. It says, "The Committee is deeply 
concerned to note that the issue of pending cases with 
262 

[16 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
the BIFR/AAIFR, which shall abate on repeal of SICA, has not been addressed 
in the above mentioned Bill. They find that the transfers, through provisions, 
are conspicuous by their absence in the proposed NCLT set up. This, the 
Committee feel, will cause a great hardship to the sick companies whose 
cases are pending before the BIFR/AAIFR and they are of the opinion, that a 
lot of time will be wasted in registering the said abated cases afresh with 
NCLT. Hence, the Committee recommends that the Government should bring 
a suitable amendment in the present B ill itself to deal with abated cases." The 
Committee says that a lot of time will be wasted in registering the said cases. 
And what will happen during this interim period till a fresh registration is 
applied or till a fresh registration is mad e? As you are aware, this registration, 
in the case of the BIFR, is 100 per cent wiping out of the capital. Here, it is 50 
per cent. So, there is no reason why any case, which is already registered with 
the BIFR, is not suitable for NCLT. 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Mr. Bagrodia, your party has got two 
speakers.   So, you divide your time accordingly. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Then, Madam, I speak when I move 
my amendments. For the time being, I will try to conclude. Madam, could you 
tell me how much time left for my party? 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: You have  started at 1407 hours. You 
have already spoken for twenty minutes and Mr. Goenka is also there to speak 
from your party. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Okay, Madam, I would just try to finish 
it. Another very important question, whic h arises here, is t hat clause 4 of the 
Repeal Bill shall be re-numbered, as sub-clause 1 thereof, and at the end of 
the said sub-clause, the following provision shall be inserted: "On the 
dissolution of the BIFR and the AIFR, t he Government has made all efforts to 
absorb the officers and employees, holding regular appointments in these 
organizations, against suitable positions in the National Company Law 
Tribunal, and its Appellate Tribunal, which had been created under the 
Companies Second Amendment Act, 2002." In brief, there is a very small 
number of regular employees - 50 or 60. Others are not regular employees in 
the BIFR. For whatever wisdom the Go vernment has decided, why should 
these workers be made to suffer; why should these employees be 
263 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2003] 
made to suffer? Why should we not make a law in this regard? Why should 
they not be absorbed in the NCLT? They have got a vast experience of 
working in such units. So, I would like to request that this should be done 
under the law with the conviction that this is a necessity. Madam, I appeal to 
the hon. Minister, through you, once more, let us not go only for assurances. 
Or, if you give an assurance on the floor  of the House that these amendments 
will be brought in the next session, I don' t mind. But let us not leave it to 
making the rules; let us not leave it only to the bureaucratic set up to do it. If it 
would not be done, there would be so many problems for everybody involved 
in this kind of set up, which, I think, the Government is not able to visualise. 
With these words, I thank you very much for giving me this opportunity. 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH (Andhra Pradesh): Thank you, Madam 
Deputy Chairman, for giving me this opportunity to speak on the Sick Industrial 
Companies (Special Provisions) Repeal Bill, 2003. This is, indeed, a welcome 
Bill. There is not much to be debated on this. This should have been brought 
long time back because nobody was confident that the BIFR -- when it had 
been constituted, the way it had been co nstituted, and the powers that had 
been conferred on it -- would be able to deliver the goods. Though it had been 
constituted some 15 years back, but it was never fully constituted. And, on 
certain occasions, I had to make a co mment that the Board of Industrial 
Finance for Reconstruction itself required reconstruction. That was the state of 
affairs. There had been umpteen cases where the units, which had been 
referred to the BIFR, had become sicker because of the inordinate delay in 
disposing of the issues. I welcome this  Bill because the performance of these 
institutions was tardy and very inefficient, and the Government was also not 
serious about strengthening this institut ion. So, I would like to request the 
Government to be serious because the sick ness in the industry is the greatest 
menace, -affecting the economy of our country. A lot of installed capacity of the 
industries is still unutilised because of  the sickness. If we analyse the reasons 
as to why the industries have become si ck, there are certain very, very small 
reasons, say, lack of raw material, lack of adequate banking facilities at 
appropriate time, lack of marketing facilities. After globalisation, there is a 
danger of more industries becoming sick, unless they fulfil certain conditions. 
That means, their products should become more competitive at the international 
level. And for this they have to improve their productivity rate and they have to 
improve the quality of the product so that they can 
264 

[16 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
compete with the international products . These are the aspects which have to 
be taken into consideration. Once a unit  becomes sick, it is  being referred to 
the BIFR. Now, it will be referred to this Tribunal, which is going to be 
constituted as per this Bill. I am very happy that this Tribunal will dispense with 
the multiplicity of fora to decide on matte rs of mergers, amalgamations, etc.  
This development, which is forthcoming, is very good. 
I want to make a suggestion to the Government. The NCLT will be 
under the control of the Company Law Board. Will this NCLT be under the 
Ministry of Finance or the under the Company Law Board? 
AN. HONOURABLE MEMBER:   Yes. 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH : That is the weakest Regulator in this 
country. The Company Law Board is the weakest Regulator in this country. 
Umpteen irregularities have been committed, but they were never checked, 
never punished. That was the root caus e for the scams in the share market 
also. It is known that the auditors have erred, the management have erred, 
and it has gone to the notice of the Company Law Board also. But, the 
existing provisions of punishment are less stringent, so, they have not taken 
any action. There are umpte en cases, but I don't want to narrate them at this 
stage. I request the Minister that more  teeth should be provided to this 
Tribunal so that they can deal with such problems effectively. 
I want to give one more suggestion. If there is an erosion of 50 per 
cent of the net worth, that can also be referred to this. That was the implication 
that I could infer. It is very good. But wh at is the definition of the net worth? 
Net worth can be easily manipulated if one is not very specific about the net 
worth and the management control. Now that the proposal is being referred to 
this Tribunal, they should come out with a package. Ultimately, who is 
responsible for the sickness of the indust ry? In most cases, the promoters are 
responsible. It is the promoters who are responsible for this. The units are 
becoming sick due to the siphoning off of the funds or the diversion of funds. 
And, as far as the other reasons like, marketing facilities, lack of material 
resources are concerned, the Government can take care of them. But when 
promoters themselves indulge in maki ng the unit sick, then, stringent 
provisions have to be made. They should come forward to the Tribunal with a 
package for revival so that 
265 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2003] 
it can be considered very effectively. 
One more suggestion, which I wanted to make, is this. If ten Benches 
are not sufficient, my request is kindly increase the number of Benches so that 
the cases can be disposed of as early as possible. Once a unit is declared as 
a sick unit, it should not remain sick for lo ng. Either it should be liquidated or it 
should be revived. The more the delay, the more the sickness and a sick unit 
cannot be revived at a subsequent time even if the Tribunal were to give an 
award for its revival. There are a number  of other BIFR orders which were not 
implemented. In my area alone, there is a one very big paper mill by the name 
Rayalaseema Paper Mill, which has been taken over by the first generation 
entrepreneur with the sole intention of  coming to the rescue of the workers 
working in that industry. Having spent Rs. 60 crores, the bankers could not 
provide working capital, and more than 38 persons have committed suicides. 
And, till today, that unit is sick. In spite of the direction of the BIFR, the bankers 
could not provide the working capital. So, they have prepared an appeal, 
which is in the preliminary stages. Unless you provide more teeth to the 
Tribunal, which is going to be constituted, I don't think, the purpose will be 
served. For example, take the case of the IDPL, the Indian Drugs and 
Pharmaceutical Limited. The hon. Mini ster is here. We made a number of 
representations to this effect. 
And it is a pioneer industry in t he field of drugs and pharmaceuticals 
in this country which has produced so many entrepreneurs like N.G. Reddy, 
Reddy Labs. So many big industrialists in pharmaceuticals have come up, but, 
till today, we have not been able to revive it. Even the most possible reasons 
which we extend to the Government have not been taken up. Sir, the 
Government's requirements in respect of pharmaceuticals can be fulfilled by 
that unit. Even then, it has not been c onsidered. So, the Government should 
be very serious. I welcome the process of  disinvestments that is being done, 
but, either you should do it quickly, or, you should provide all these industries 
with some budgetary support. No production is taking place. Every year, about 
Rs.100-150 crores, you have to spend to provide budgetary support to these 
units. This is merely a waste of public money. So, my request is either o revive 
it or disinvest it immediately so that  public money can be saved. One more 
point I would like to make is this. A fter these units become sick, one aspect is 
we have to see how to revive it; how to do this?   But you should ascertain 
what are 
266 

[16 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
the reasons for these units becoming sick. As I told you, most of the capital of 
the banks is in these industries. And,  once upon a time, though small-scale 
industries in this country used to comprise a major chunk of the exports, 
nowadays, they are not competitive with  the international market. They need 
to upgrade their technologies so that their products become more competitive 
in respect of cost and quality. Sir, the in puts or the cost of production, except 
labour, is abnormally high in this country. But when we go in for large-scale 
production and automation, the componen t of labour cost becomes irrelevant. 
It is high time the Government pondered over this. 
Sir, we are in a transitional stage. We have taken a decision for 
globalisation, or privatis ation. My apprehension is, most of the industries are 
becoming sick because the Government has not provided sufficient time or 
cushion to enable them to be more co mpetitive, as per the international 
standards. In this process, there are going to be more NPAs also. Sir, this 
aspect has to be taken into consideration. Sir, I welcome this Bill. With 
whatever experiences you have gained in the BIFR, kindly make this Tribunal 
more effective.   Thank you. 
DR. L.M. SINGHVI (Rajasthan): Ma dam, the Bill deserves to be 
welcomed and I am happy that the House has been able to find time to 
discuss this Bill which has been pending for nearly two years. The sick 
undertakings have become more sick, but, I think the diagnosis on the basis 
of which this Bill was brought is for everyone to endorse and to understand. 
Sickness, Madam, is not always becaus e of the people who run the business; 
is also because of them because some of them are too selfish and have been 
found to enrich themselves at the cost of the unit itself. On the other hand, 
sickness has been caused partly because of the inept way in which the banks 
have handled many of these undertakings. It is of the greatest importance for 
us to put in place an alternative mech anism as provided, that the National 
Company Law Tribunal will now be vested with the authority to deal with this 
phenomenon of sickness. I do hope that they are able to cope with it. The past 
record shows that the National Company Law Tribunal or the Company Law 
Tribunal which was existing before, was also clogged and congested. It is also 
important to bear in mind that the lit igious approach will not do; one has to 
adopt a problem-solving approach and that is why this diagnosis should 
commend itself to the House. The slow pace of BIFR intervention has become 
notorious, and, I think, it is 
267 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2003) 
partly because of that that  the problem of sickness was not really tackled with 
economically but remained in the corridors of litigious approach to the 
problem. 
It is also correct that there was little monitoring of sanctioned revival 
schemes, and there were also delay in winding up schemes. But, Madam, I 
think, what the hon. Member, Mr. Santos h Bagrodia, has raised by way of an 
amendment and in the course of his speech ought to commend itself to the 
Government for their consideration. It is not the fault of those who were before 
the Tribunal or the Appellate Authorit y under the SICA of 1985. They have 
been waiting for some solution to emerge, and if time and resources have 
been invested in that process and effort should be made to see that they are 
brought to a conclusion, I have a feel ing that Mr. Bagrodia's own amendment 
may not achieve the purpose he has in mind because he does allow for 
abatement in the first place and then pr ovides by a non-obstante clause, not 
standing the repeal, they will be dealt with. A way can be found by the 
Government to make sure that those proceedings to which he refers to in 
clauses two and three by way of his amendments are pr otected and those 
which are already undergoing these hearings and trying to find a solution do 
not have to start de novo. But if they are asked to start de novo, all that time 
would have been wasted, and, in fac t, a lot of time has been wasted both 
before the Board and the Appellate Authority. This institution will go, in my 
respectful submission, unlamented and un sung because it took too long to 
deal with problems of sickness, the sickness which was before them got more 
sick, and, I think, it is important that  the Government is now taking up this 
issue in a way in which, I hope, the pr oblem of sickness will be expeditiously 
dealt with. It is possible that the National Company Law Board may also find 
the problem of litigiousness of long an d protracted and agonising procedures, 
but I think, when all is said and done,  the point made by Mr. Santosh Bagrodia 
about those pending proceedings particularly after an undertaking has been 
declared as a sick undertaking ought somehow to be rescued in terms of 
saving the time for solving their problems. The banks and the other players in 
the system should also be encouraged to sustain units and to make them 
functional and flourish rather than to apply this squeeze, the only thing that 
they have known in the past. 
I congratulate the hon. Finance Minister for the brighter prospects for 
our economy.   I also congratulate him for having brought this Bill to deal 
268 

(16 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
with the problem of sickness in a more effective, in a more expeditious and in 
a more purposeful manner.   Thank you, Madam. 
SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Madam, I wish I 
could have also congratulated the Finance Minister, but, I am sorry, I would 
not be able to do so. Madam, I am afraid certain points which I am going to 
raise here would be repetition of what has been said from our side during the 
discussion on the National Company Law Tribunal Bill which was passed by 
this House. But I am constrained to point out one point. We are not discussing 
here the winding up of the BIFR. What we  are discussing is the Sick Industrial 
Companies (Special Provisions) Repeal Bill, 2001, a Bill to repeal the Sick 
Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985. I am sure the whole 
House should again ponder over the ob jectives of that Bill because the 
objectives have changed so far as this Bill is concerned, the National Law 
Tribunal Bill. Its objective was that the sickness, for the first time, in this 
country was, at least, identified not as a credit and debit and the restructuring 
part, but, that the industrial sickness has its own social and economic 
implications. That was understood when this Bill was framed. But, somehow 
or the other, the objectives of that Bill  as a social and economic implications 
have been changed. If you compare the report of the Justice Eradi Committee 
with this Bill, I can say that the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) 
Repeal Bill, 2001 is not for expeditious revival of sick units. 
It is for expeditious closure of sick units. Now, the objective of the 
earlier Bill, if I remember the words correctly, the main objective, was the 
utilization of the capital assets, the productive assets. And somehow, Madam, 
the country is forgetting the producti ve assets. Ours may be a voice in 
wilderness, but we will go on, as Mr. Jibon Roy had done in the morning. 
Now, the productive assets include the capital, material and labour. 
Our perception is, the thinking that is prevalent now is, the protection of the 
capital, and labour is not on the agenda. When I say 'labour', it does not mean 
the sacking of some people or winding up of companies. The social 
implications have to be foreseen in those places where sickness has been 
there. Industrial sickness is on the rise. Can anyone deny that? 
Now, as Dr. Singhvi was saying -- and it is also a fact -- if one goes 
through the RBI figures, one will find that  most of the closures and sickness 
were caused by policies, by the promoters, and first three per by 
269 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December. 2003] 
industrial sickness. But what is being stressed today is that it is the labour, it is 
the labour and it is the labour, more labour and labour productivity! But facts 
do not state that! 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF AGRO AND 
RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRI SANGH PRIYA GAUTAM) : That is what Shri 
Bagrodia was also stating. 
SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE : No, Sir, I am not talking about that 
issue. 
SHRI SANGH PRIYA GAUTAM : Labour-oriented units are falling 
sick. 
SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE : I am not talking about that. If you 
so wish, you can go there and see for yourself. What I am saying is, this is the 
philosophy. The philosophy behind the re peal of SICA is not to improve the 
working of the AAIFR cases. So far as  BIFR cases are concerned, it is the 
same thing again. BIFR did not have any mandatory power to revive an 
industry. It had the mandatory power to wind up an industry! BIFR's weakness 
was that, time is the essence of re vival, but that was not taken into 
consideration. Section 22 was defective; everyone has been talking about that 
for years together. So, the objectives were there, but they were not 
implemented. 
Today, the repeal by this Bill cannot and will not cause any 
improvement, because sickness is on t he increase. The Government cannot 
come and say that with the liquidation of BIFR, the NCLT will be on a binge to 
reduce the sickness. I don't think anyone can say what exactly is being 
achieved, as the National Compan y Law Tribunals will have the same 
problems as BIFR had. It will be the same. So many cases will be there. 
Already so many figures have been given in this context and I don't want to 
repeat those figures. The question is not only that. The question would be the 
expeditious closure of the units through this, because they would have more 
legal powers. 
So, the fact remains that the basic reasons for sickness, the 
diagnosis of sickness, are not being addr essed. The basic problem is that in 
implementing any measure by revival of units, time is the essence, and that 
270 

[16 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
objective, that essence, t hat urgency is not there. The urgency is probably to 
save some capital, the creditors' units. 
If you go through the Statement of Objects and Reasons, the first 
paragraph, a, b, c, d, e & f, deals with delays in winding up of sick units. Yes, 
delays in winding up of sick companies. That is the major objective for the 
repealing of the earlier Act, and bringing up the National Company Law 
Tribunal. It never addresses the delays in revival of units. So, revival is not the 
agenda 'but closure or winding up is the ag enda. If that is the case, so far as 
this Bill is concerned, after the National Company Law Tribunal comes into 
force, BIFR becomes redundant. Still, coming to the philosophical change so 
far as the Government is concerned, I have to again remind them, at least 
think about the social implications of expeditious closure of these units. The 
social implications, the economic implicat ions, the political fall-out, everything, 
will have to be taken into consideration. 
Madam, the last point which I want to stress upon is, what has been 
told from his own point of view, regar ding the procedures that BIFR and 
AAIFR would follow. Let the Government be clear, because if time is the 
essence, the question of registering the cases --which include old cases 
also— would mean that we have already got the obituaries written and we just 
want to repeal certain procedural matters, legal matters. We are not interested 
in that. The fact is that if the cases pe nding in the BIFR have to be registered 
again, that means you have written the obituaries for all these units already! 
My second point is if the Government has even five per cent interest 
in the revival of industries, I would like to know what exactly is the guideline 
from the Government regarding the sa nctioned schemes for the sick units. 
Unfortunately, in our St ate, we have a few units where the revival schemes 
have already been sanctioned. 
Now this non-implementation of the sanctioned scheme has also 
been the reason for closure of various units. That being the case, how the new 
agency is going to take up them? What type of assurance the Government can 
give that, at least, this sanctioned revival scheme would not suffer because of 
the changeover from this BIFR to National Company Law Tribunal? So far as 
the cases which are pending with the Draft Revival Scheme are concerned, we 
can talk of three cases.  The first is sanctioned 
271 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2003] 
scheme. How many sanctioned schemes is BIFR right now monitoring? What 
will happen to them? Second, whether the Draft Revival Scheme has already 
been prepared with BIFR and what is going to be the procedure? Third, if the 
cases are registered, taking the time into  consideration, is the Government at 
all keen on giving any sort of guidelines to the National Company Law 
Tribunal? Madam, I know the requirement. No-holds-bar, now it is very clear. I 
know that it is in the interest of the capital. The Government has to act now. I 
can only say, it does not serve the inte rest of the labour. I do not say labour 
means only the labour, workers, the managers and the engineers. I know 
some of the units where engineers are also managers. They have nothing to 
do with policy. The policy which we are adopting now, with this economic 
policy, the sickness is bound to increase. If the Government is serious about 
the sickness, then this is not the way. I can only indicate one particular 
example. I have seen one draft or Act in Gujarat where the State Government 
is interfering by making a Board for addr essing the problem of sick and small-
sector industries, whereas the BIFR deals with big and medium-scale 
industries. If sickness is a social problem, this is not the answer to it. If 
sickness is an economic problem, this is not the answer to it. If sickness revival 
is a part of utilisation of the capital assets, and if you treat, apart from capital 
and men, market policies also as part of th at, this is not a solutton. This is not 
going to solve anything.   Thank you.

Governor is now allowed to choose a nominee for the State Election

experienced a lot of hue and cry and there we re a lot of agitations, specially in

created a lot of emotional upheaval am ong many tribes, more so since it

are sensitive areas, which need to be ta ken into consideration. And I appeal 
that this should be taken into consider ation very seriously. Right from the 
beginning, we know that, in view of the political expediency, the State had

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Progress on action taken pursuant to the recommendations of the Joint 
Parliamentary Committee on Stock Market Scam 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): Mr. Vice-Chairman,  Sir, I am glad to submit to the 
House, a progress report on the action  pursuant to the JPC recommendations. 
The JPC had submitted its report on 19.12.2002. The Action Taken Report 
(ATR) was presented on 9 th May, 2003, that is, well within the period of six 
months. As desired by the JPC, the Government will continue to submit 
periodic reports of action taken, at six-m onthly intervals until full satisfaction of 
the Parliament. 
The Government has greatly benefit ed from the JPC's deliberations 
and expresses its gratitude to the Committ ee for Its wide-ranging and valuable 
suggestions. While certain legislative measures such as the amendment of 
SEBI Act, and repeal of UTI Act, have already come into effect, other 
proposals like the amendment to the Secu rities Contract (Regulations) Act for 
ensuring demutualisation and corporat isation of stock exchanges and 
amendment of the Banking Regulations Act for better regulation of Cooperative 
Banks are before the Parliament. The Government is also considering bringing 
about other legislations like the Co mpany Law (Amendment) Bill and the 
Government Securities Bill, 2003. 
Sir, between the last Action Tak en Report and the present one, a 
number of measures have been taken, wh ich include setting up of additional 
institutional mechanisms to keep a regular watch on the financial markets, 
establishment of a co-ordination mechan ism with regulators and investigating 
agencies, reference to SEBI regarding the secondary market investment 
decisions of the UTI in 89 companies identified by Tarapore Committee, setting 
up of Serious Frauds Invest igation Office, etc. While  some recommendations 
are pending for want of legislative mandat es, others can   be   implemented   
only   after  the   current  investigations  or  judicial

developments on a continuous basis and there has been a good progress in
